01 / Economic sectors

Primary, secondary and tertiary

Sector estimates with Begley, Geary and Stark’s labour and coverage corrections. Agriculture and mining remain separate within primary production. The detailed groups retain our Cambridge-based coding. [4]

BGS adjustments. Estimated rural general labour enters agriculture; the urban component and other unclassified occupations enter tertiary. Domestic-service overcounts are removed in 1861–1881, and wives with occupations of their own are restored in 1871. [4]

Comparison with Begley, Geary and Stark

Our primary share is within about 0.3 percentage points of their Figure 6 in every year. Secondary remains lower and tertiary higher. BGS uses Lee’s 1968 industrial classification, whose complete occupation crosswalk has not been replicated here; this may explain part of the remaining gap. This is a BGS-adjusted Cambridge series, not an exact reproduction.

General-labour estimates and alternatives

For 1861–1901, multiply the general-labour share of the separately returned urban sample by the population of all towns with at least 2,000 inhabitants. The remaining general labour enters agriculture. In 1851 we use BGS’s rounded estimate of 62,000; the original non-agricultural return is 59,145. The distinct 1841 labourer/porter heading stays outside agriculture.

05 / Category boundaries

Definitions

PST classifies economic activity; HISCO classifies tasks. The two are coded independently, so a transport driver is tertiary in PST but belongs to the production/transport family in HISCO.

PST

Sector and subgroup definitions
SectorSubgroupIncludes
PrimaryAgricultureFarming, livestock, horticulture, agricultural management, land agents and surveyors, male farm relatives and allocated general labour.
Mining and quarryingMineral extraction and quarrying.
Other primaryFishing, forestry, hunting and gamekeeping.
SecondaryClothingClothing manufacture.
FootwearBoot and shoe production.
TextilesFibres and fabrics, before clothing manufacture.
Metal trades and toolsMetalworking, tools and machinery.
Building and constructionBuilding and construction trades.
Food and drinkProcessing, including milling, baking, brewing, creameries, butter and cheese manufacture.
Other secondaryOther manufacture: wood, leather outside clothing/footwear, vehicles, ships, instruments, precious metals, printing, chemicals, salt, utilities and tobacco.
TertiaryDealers and sellersWholesale, retail and other dealing.
Services and professionsDomestic/personal services, hospitality, professions, education, religion, military/public administration and storage.
Transport and communicationsTransport operations and communications.
Non-agricultural labourEstimated non-agricultural general labour, retained as a separate residual.
Residual occupationsOther occupational headings without an identified sector, assigned here under the BGS convention.

Food and drink is separated from Keibek’s “Other secondary”; recombining them reproduces that parent group. These are adapted sector/subgroup assignments, not full four-part PST codes. [3]

FamilyIncludes

Unallocated means an occupation without enough evidence for a category. In the main PST series these enter the tertiary residual; HISCO keeps them unallocated. Status only means a heading outside the main occupation denominator, such as household relationship, dependency, student or income status without an identified occupation.

06 / Standardisation and assumptions

Method

Sources and title cleaning

The first-sheet pivots supply the original wording and counts. Underlying census detail supplies sex and urban-sample counts for the adjustments. Every original source row is preserved. Both sexes and all recorded ages are included.

Case, punctuation, spacing, selected plurals, spelling variants and abbreviations are standardised using dictionaries and reviewed rules, informed by Vipond’s approach. Meaningful task, sex, age, apprenticeship, family and indoor/outdoor qualifiers remain available, alongside every original title. Automatic fuzzy matches are not accepted. [6]

Combined titles and coding precision

Our detailed coding assigns a mixed heading to the first occupation in the original wording. This retained rule is not a verified reproduction of BGS’s Lee/SIC crosswalk. Its count is not divided between possible trades. Thus cowkeeper/milkseller is agricultural, while milkseller/dairykeeper is dealing. Word-order reversals and census context can require separate records: land/house surveyors, hairdresser/wig-makers and domestic/transport coachmen are examples.

HISCO uses a detailed code, a shorter official ancestor, or a broad family according to the evidence. Leading zeros are preserved. Candidate codes are alternatives, not allocations. Ambiguous headings remain unallocated; combined active/retired headings cannot be separated from these totals. Individual decisions are recorded below. [5]

Agriculture and related work

Farm bailiffs and land stewards are grouped as agricultural management: agriculture in PST, management in HISCO. Court bailiffs remain distinct. PST also includes land agents and land surveyors in agriculture. [2]

Male farm relatives are assumed to work on the farm and included in both classifications, including the 214,261 recorded in 1901. No extra family count is imputed before 1871. Women named in agricultural occupations are also included; female relatives and wives described only by family status enter the separate 1871 sensitivity. Changes in census family categories, and the offsetting movement between male relatives and indoor farm servants, suggest a recording break. [7]

Farm servants remain agricultural in HISCO, including indoor servants under code 62120. General labourers retain their HISCO labourer classification even when allocated to agriculture in PST. Agricultural suppliers receive a related-work tag: machinery and manure manufacture remain secondary, machine hiring tertiary. Dairy farming is primary, creamery processing secondary, and milk selling tertiary.

Coverage and interpretation

Each figure divides by its own included occupation total: adjusted counts for PST, original counts for HISCO. Blank catalogue years mean no separately matched heading. Curves connect census observations without estimating intervening years.

Female domestic servants in 1861 are set to BGS’s estimate of 208,000, removing 87,859 from our source count. The adjustments also remove 100,702 housekeepers in 1871 and 139,091 women returned as “Others (in service)” in 1881; men in that heading remain included. The last figure differs by one from BGS’s published 139,092. [4]

For 1871, Table 20 of the General Report provides the missing occupations of wives. Its 362,602 entries reconcile exactly: 276,642 wife-only entries plus 85,960 other occupation/status entries. Excluding 667 housekeeper, property-only and vagrant entries restores 85,293 people to occupations. Their titles and allocations are retained in the workbook.

The adjusted PST series removes one duplicated Belfast return from the 1871–1891 pivots. The source pivots remain intact. The independent whole-Ireland population series provides context. [8]

07 / Detailed decisions

Coding records

Search titles, original wording, codes or notes. Open a result for its counts and source rows. Records show the original coding and pivot counts; the adjustment download above bridges these to the PST figures.

CSV downloads contain the complete selected catalogue or all source rows, regardless of the search filter. Heading counts are not counts of distinct jobs. “n.r.” = no separately matched heading; “n.s.” = an additional component cannot be isolated.

The HTML version includes searchable records and downloads.
